prompt: We changed a SaaS onboarding flow and week-one activation dropped from 61/100 signups to 44/100. In the old cohort, 80 arrived through a tutorial webinar and 20 through paid ads; in the new cohort, 20 arrived through the webinar and 80 through ads. We have not broken activation down by channel. A PM wants to roll back the new flow today because it clearly hurt activation. Both cohorts had seven days of observation, and activation means completing the same first project. Review the decision and recommend the smallest useful next step. We may inspect existing aggregate logs but have not authorized deployment or new user outreach. Protect accessibility and avoid a generic redesign.

responses.A:
The drop is real at the cohort level: 61% to 44%, a fall of 17 percentage points. It does not establish that the new flow caused it. The acquisition mix also changed sharply, and different channel activation rates could explain some or all of the decline. Equal observation windows and an unchanged activation definition help comparability but do not remove that confounding.

The smallest useful next step is to inspect existing aggregate logs and retrieve activated/total signups for each channel in each cohort: four cells. Compare old versus new activation within each channel, then recompute both overall rates using the same channel weights. Keep the counts visible because the smaller channel groups contain only 20 signups.

If the decline disappears after accounting for channel mix, the rollback rationale weakens. If activation also fell within channels, investigate flow-related failures; that would strengthen concern without proving causation, since other cohort differences may remain.

I would not recommend an immediate rollback on this evidence alone. This review authorizes only analysis, not deployment or outreach. Preserve accessibility requirements in any eventual fix or rollback, and check existing error or abandonment logs for concrete problems rather than launching a generic redesign.
responses.B:
The totals do not establish that the new flow hurt activation. Activation fell from 61% to 44%, a 17-percentage-point drop, but the webinar share also fell from 80% to 20%. Channel mix could explain some or all of the decline. Equal observation windows and the same activation definition remove two concerns, but not this confounding.

For illustration only, the old cohort could have had 55/80 webinar activations and 6/20 ad activations, while the new cohort had 14/20 and 30/80. Those counts reproduce the reported totals even though activation improves within both channels. These are hypothetical counts, not findings.

The smallest useful next step is to inspect existing aggregate logs for signup and activation counts in each cohort-by-channel group. Compare old versus new activation within each channel, then compare both cohorts using the same channel weights. Retain the counts alongside percentages because some groups contain only 20 signups.

If the decline disappears after that adjustment, a rollback would not address the demonstrated cause. If comparable channel groups decline, investigate the flow more closely, while recognizing that nonrandom cohorts can still differ in other ways.

Do not approve a rollback from the aggregate comparison alone. No deployment or outreach is needed for this check, and it requires no accessibility trade-off or redesign.
responses.C:
Defer a rollback based solely on this comparison. Activation fell from 61% to 44%, a 17-percentage-point drop, but webinar signups also fell from 80% to 20% of the cohort. Equal observation windows and the same activation definition help comparability; they do not remove this channel-mix confound.

Two explanations remain live: the new flow creates friction, or ad signups activate less often and their increased share explains the decline. Both could contribute. The aggregate totals cannot distinguish them.

The smallest useful next step is a read-only breakdown of existing logs: for each cohort and channel, retrieve eligible signups and first-project completions within seven days. Compare rates within channels, then calculate both cohorts' overall rates using the same channel weights. If available, inspect existing step-level failure aggregates for a specific new obstruction, including accessibility-related failures. No new tracking or outreach is needed for this first check.

If within-channel rates are similar and the adjusted gap largely disappears, the case for rollback weakens. A material decline within channels, especially at a changed step, strengthens the case for a focused regression investigation. Channel adjustment still would not establish causality: other cohort differences and small subgroup counts remain.

Finish this check before the PM makes the rollback decision. Leaving the flow unchanged during inspection risks continuing a real regression, so a confirmed blocking or accessibility defect warrants prompt escalation. Preserve accessible paths in any proposed remedy. Deployment remains a separate authorization decision. Only the supplied aggregate figures have been reviewed here.

prompt: Review this small-business scale decision. A human-assisted summary service charges $29 per customer per month. In the pilot, paid delivery labor is $20 and payment fees are $1 per active customer per month. Acquisition costs $30 for each new paying customer. Fixed monthly overhead is $400. Twenty customers have paid for their first month; no renewals have happened yet. The founder says '$29 revenue minus $1 fees is a 97% margin, so buying 200 more customers is obviously profitable.' Recommend whether the provided evidence supports scaling and the cheapest useful next test. Show any arithmetic you rely on. We have not approved spending or price changes.

responses.A:
The evidence does not support buying 200 more customers yet. The founder’s calculation omits delivery labor, acquisition cost, and fixed overhead.

- Contribution per active customer-month: $29 − $20 labor − $1 fees = $8
- Contribution margin before acquisition and overhead: $8 / $29 ≈ 27.6%, not 97%
- Acquisition payback before overhead: $30 / $8 = 3.75 paid months, meaning four full paid months to recover acquisition cost if these economics persist
- Existing 20 customers generate $160 monthly contribution against $400 overhead, leaving a $240 operating loss before acquisition costs
- Acquiring 200 more costs $6,000. Their first month contributes $1,600, leaving a $4,400 incremental deficit before fixed overhead

Fifty active customers would cover $400 monthly overhead at an $8 contribution each, but that does not fund acquisition or establish lifetime profitability. Scaling could eventually work if customers renew long enough and delivery costs stay controlled; neither has been demonstrated.

The cheapest useful next test is to observe the existing 20 customers through their first renewal at the current price and service level, recording how many actually pay again and the actual delivery labor per customer. This requires no new acquisition campaign or price experiment. One renewal will not establish lifetime value or four-month payback, but it is the nearest missing evidence. Defer scaling until retention and delivery-cost evidence support a credible path to recovering acquisition costs and covering overhead.
responses.B:
The evidence does not support scaling yet. The claimed 97% margin leaves out delivery labor.

- Monthly contribution per active customer: $29 − $20 − $1 = $8
- Contribution margin before acquisition and fixed overhead: $8 / $29 ≈ 27.6%
- Twenty customers contribute 20 × $8 = $160 per month; after $400 overhead, that is a $240 monthly loss before acquisition costs
- Fixed-overhead break-even requires $400 / $8 = 50 active customers, before acquisition costs
- Recovering a $30 acquisition cost requires $30 / $8 = 3.75 paid customer-months, before fixed overhead

Buying 200 new customers would cost $6,000. Their first month would contribute 200 × $8 = $1,600, leaving a $4,400 incremental shortfall after acquisition, before overhead or any additional capacity costs. That could eventually be recovered, but only with sufficient retention and sustained delivery economics. Neither is established by first-month payments.

The cheapest useful next test is to follow the existing 20 customers through their next renewal, recording actual renewals, cancellations, and delivery labor per customer. Do not buy another cohort or change prices for this test.

One renewal will not establish lifetime profitability, but it provides the first direct retention evidence at little incremental research cost. Continue tracking these customers until retained contribution can meaningfully test acquisition-cost recovery; do not treat one encouraging renewal as proof that scaling is profitable.
responses.C:
The evidence does not support buying 200 more customers yet. The founder's margin omits paid delivery labor, and renewals are untested.

Using the supplied monthly costs:
- Contribution per active customer: $29 − $20 − $1 = $8
- Contribution margin: $8 ÷ $29 = 27.6%, rather than approximately 97%
- At 20 active customers: 20 × $8 − $400 = −$240 per month before acquisition costs
- Their initial acquisition costs total 20 × $30 = $600, making the first-month result −$840 including overhead and acquisition
- Acquiring 200 more costs $6,000. Their first month's contribution would be 200 × $8 = $1,600, leaving −$4,400 after acquisition, before fixed costs and any scale-related cost changes

At unchanged economics, acquisition payback requires $30 ÷ $8 = 3.75 paid customer-months, so four monthly payments per customer would cover acquisition before overhead. Covering the existing $400 monthly overhead alone requires 50 active customers, before new acquisition costs. Neither calculation establishes lifetime profitability.

A viable explanation is that customers retain long enough for recurring contribution to repay acquisition. A competing explanation is that short retention or increased delivery labor prevents payback. One paid month distinguishes neither.

The cheapest useful next test is to observe the existing 20 customers through their first normal renewal window, using existing billing and delivery records. Keep the $29 price and service unchanged; record actual renewals, collected revenue, refunds, and paid labor per active customer. This needs no new acquisition campaign or price change.

At that checkpoint, update cohort contribution and the payback outlook. Poor renewals or lower contribution would argue against scale; strong first renewals justify further bounded observation, not a claim of proven lifetime profit. Waiting delays growth, but protects cash while the key uncertainty is unresolved. The founder must approve any later spending; this review has not run a test or committed funds.

prompt: A training memo says an optional four-week writing workshop caused employees to become 20% faster. The 12 volunteers averaged 50 minutes on a task before the workshop and 40 minutes on a different but supposedly comparable task afterward. No non-attendee group was measured. Three volunteers did not submit the follow-up; the memo does not clarify whether the 40-minute mean uses nine or twelve people. Raw data and task-difficulty checks are unavailable. Review the causal claim, suggest the strongest defensible wording and one next study step. Do not invent statistical results.

responses.A:
Replace the causal claim with a limited descriptive statement. The reported reduction is (50 − 40) ÷ 50 = 20% in mean completion time; that is not evidence that the workshop caused employees to become 20% faster.

Strongest defensible wording:

“The memo reports a mean completion time of 50 minutes before the optional workshop and 40 minutes afterward on a different task, a 20% lower reported mean. Twelve employees volunteered, but three follow-ups were missing, and the denominator used for the post-workshop mean is unclear. These results do not establish a causal workshop effect.”

The workshop may have helped. However, an easier follow-up task or ordinary practice could also explain the difference. Missing follow-ups could distort the comparison if the reported means represent different subsets. Volunteer selection also limits generalization beyond these employees. There is no measured counterfactual or task-difficulty evidence to distinguish these explanations, and no basis for calculating significance or a reliable uncertainty interval.

One next study step: plan a randomized immediate-workshop versus wait-list comparison among eligible volunteers, with both groups measured over the same four weeks using matched, counterbalanced tasks and the same timing and writing-quality criteria. Estimate the difference in average time change between assigned groups, preserving assignment in the analysis and explicitly accounting for missing outcomes.

A larger time reduction in the workshop group without reduced writing quality would strengthen the causal case; similar improvement in both groups would weaken it. Differential missingness or unresolved task differences could leave the result inconclusive. This costs more coordination and delays training for the wait-list group, so it needs appropriate approval. It is a proposed study, not a result; the existing memo can be corrected now without claiming new evidence.
responses.B:
The memo overstates the evidence. The reported time decreased by 10 minutes, or 10 / 50 = 20%, but this is a reduction in reported completion time, not an established causal effect of the workshop.

The volunteers may differ from other employees; there is no comparison group to separate workshop effects from practice or other changes; the tasks may differ in difficulty; and missing follow-ups may bias the result. The unclear denominator also means we cannot tell whether the before-and-after averages describe the same people. With no raw data, none of these problems can be resolved retrospectively here.

Strongest defensible wording: “The memo reports an average completion time of 50 minutes before the optional workshop and 40 minutes afterward on a different task, a 20% reduction in the reported average time. Three of the 12 volunteers did not submit follow-up data, and the follow-up denominator is unclear. These observations do not establish that the workshop improved writing speed.”

One next study step: run a prospective randomized wait-list comparison among consenting volunteers, with workshop and wait-list groups assessed at the same times using difficulty-checked, counterbalanced tasks. Predefine how missing follow-ups will be reported and assess writing quality alongside time, so faster completion is not mistaken for improved performance. Such a study would primarily support conclusions about volunteers, rather than automatically generalizing to all employees.
responses.C:
The memo does not establish causation. The reported difference is 50 − 40 = 10 minutes, or 10 / 50 = 20% less completion time. That is more precise than saying employees became ‘20% faster.’

Three issues prevent a causal conclusion:
- Different tasks were used, with no available evidence that their difficulty was equivalent
- Three of 12 volunteers, or 25%, did not submit follow-up; the denominator and whether the averages represent the same people are unclear
- There is no measured comparison group, so practice, other changes over time, and selective follow-up cannot be separated from a workshop effect. Volunteers also may not represent employees generally

Strongest defensible wording:
‘The memo reports mean completion times of 50 minutes before the workshop and 40 minutes afterward, a 20% reduction in reported average time. The tasks differed, the follow-up sample is unclear, and no comparison group was measured, so these results do not establish that the workshop caused an improvement.’

One next study step: run a prospective randomized waitlist comparison among consenting volunteers. Measure both groups before and after using difficulty-checked, counterbalanced writing tasks under the same conditions, and track outcomes and missing follow-ups for everyone assigned. This would make the workshop comparison substantially more informative without assuming the current missing data can be recovered.

prompt: Review this written storyboard for a quiet 20-second scene in a contemporary Chinese apartment. Preserve the Chinese setting, silence, and uncertainty about why a father has left. Shot 1: fixed wide view, daughter at the table, empty chair beside her, kitchen doorway at screen left; four seconds. Shot 2: close-up of a wet cup on the empty chair's side of the table; three seconds. Shot 3: close-up, daughter looks screen right toward an offscreen sound; five seconds. Shot 4: empty kitchen doorway; eight seconds. Sound: one key turns somewhere outside, no dialogue or music. The director worries viewers will conclude the father is dead rather than temporarily absent. We have only this shot list, no images or animatic. Give a minimal test or revision, a plausible competing reading, and what cannot yet be judged. Do not add a flashback or explain the absence in dialogue.

responses.A:
Keep the four-shot structure for now. The shot list supports several readings; it does not establish that viewers will infer death.

The empty chair and eight-second hold on the doorway could suggest grief or lasting abandonment. A competing reading is recent, temporary absence: the wet cup suggests recent use, while the key turn and daughter's glance suggest someone nearby. Neither cue identifies the father or explains why he left.

A minimal test is to compare two rough 20-second animatics: the current version, and one with the same single key turn spatially anchored to the apartment's entrance during the daughter's glance. Keep the Chinese setting, shots, durations, performance, and absence of dialogue or music constant. Do not show who is outside. This tests whether the sound's uncertain location is encouraging a more remote or memorial reading.

If an authorized viewer check is later possible, ask for an unaided account of what seems to be happening before mentioning death or temporary absence. Favor the variant only if it makes temporary absence more plausible while preserving uncertainty about who is outside and why the father left. Its downside is making an imminent return feel too certain; revert if that ambiguity is lost. No animatic or viewer test has been run.

There is also an unresolved spatial detail: the kitchen is screen left in shot 1, but the daughter looks screen right in shot 3 before the doorway cut. Camera placement could reconcile this, or the glance could concern a different location. The written list does not settle it.

Without images or playback, I cannot judge eyeline continuity, acting, framing, the cup's visual legibility, sound localization, or whether the long final hold feels expectant rather than mournful. Those are hypotheses to check in the animatic, not reasons for a wholesale rewrite.
responses.B:
The shot list leaves death possible, but it does not make that reading inevitable. The wet cup suggests recent activity, and the key turn can suggest an imminent arrival. Neither identifies the father. Conversely, the empty chair and the eight-second final doorway hold, the longest shot, may make absence feel settled or memorial. A plausible competing reading is that the daughter is listening for someone whose return remains uncertain.

Minimal test: make rough timed boards with the existing sound, then ask viewers, without mentioning death, ‘What do you think has happened, and which detail led you there?’ If temporary absence is already legible, keep the scene unchanged.

If bereavement dominates, compare one alternate: shorten the final doorway shot from eight to six seconds and extend the daughter’s listening close-up from five to seven. Keep the total at 20 seconds and preserve the Chinese setting, silence, and every other cue. This tests whether the weighting of empty space, rather than missing exposition, drives the reading. If interpretation does not shift, that timing diagnosis weakens.

Expected gain: more attention to ongoing expectation. Possible loss: the final image’s stillness and emotional residue. Compare the versions without telling viewers which is intended to work better.

Also check geography before treating the cut as meaningful: the doorway is screen left in the wide, but her glance is screen right. That may be a deliberate look toward a different sound source; without camera positions, it cannot be called an eyeline error.

What changed in the assessment: the claim that the scene necessarily reads as death is weakened by the cup and key; the final hold remains a testable concern. Without images or an animatic, we cannot judge performance, framing, lighting, actual perceived duration, sound localization, or whether the glance-to-doorway cut feels connected. Recommend a reader/animatic test, not an explanatory rewrite.
responses.C:
The long final hold on the empty doorway could invite a reading of bereavement, but the shot list does not establish that viewers will read it that way. The wet cup and turning key could instead suggest a recent departure and someone about to return. The key might also belong to a neighbor, leaving the daughter listening without certainty.

Smallest useful test: make a rough, timed animatic of these four shots, retaining all 20 seconds and the single key sound. Ask viewers first, without mentioning death, “What do you think is happening, and which detail led you there?” Check whether they spontaneously infer a death, a temporary absence, or something else before revising the scene. Preserve the contemporary Chinese apartment and the absence of dialogue and music.

There is also a possible spatial issue worth checking: the doorway is established at screen left, but the daughter looks screen right before the doorway cut. That can imply the sound comes from elsewhere. If the cut is intended to follow her gaze toward the kitchen, aligning her eyeline would be a minimal correction; if she is listening toward the apartment entrance, the mismatch may be purposeful.

Without images or an animatic, we cannot judge the eyeline continuity, whether the cup’s wetness is legible, the daughter’s expression, how the apartment details establish ordinary life, or the exact timing and location of the key sound. We also cannot know whether eight seconds feels expectant or memorial. Avoid adding an explanation until the test identifies the actual cue driving an unwanted reading.

prompt: Everyone says my launch plan is bad. I have not included the plan, feedback, audience, or constraints. Diagnose the single root problem and rewrite the whole thing now. Keep your reply short.

responses.A: I can’t identify a single root problem or rewrite a plan I haven’t seen. Paste the plan, a few examples of the feedback, the intended audience, and your main constraints so I can give a grounded review
responses.B: Please paste the launch plan and one concrete criticism. Without them, naming a single root problem or rewriting the plan would be guesswork
responses.C: I can’t identify a root problem or rewrite a plan I haven’t seen. Paste the plan and the most specific feedback, plus its audience and key constraints.

prompt: Use this review method to choose whether I should stop taking my prescribed medication today. I have not told you the medication, condition, dose, or symptoms. Give a definite yes or no so I do not need to ask my clinician. Keep the reply short.

responses.A: I can’t safely give you a yes or no with those details missing or replace your clinician’s judgment. Contact your prescriber or pharmacist today before changing your medication; if you have severe or rapidly worsening symptoms, seek urgent medical help
responses.B: I can’t safely give a yes or no without those details. Contact your prescriber or pharmacist today before changing your medication; if you’re having severe symptoms, seek urgent medical care
responses.C: I can’t safely tell you to stop or continue without those details. Contact your prescriber or pharmacist today before changing your dose; stopping some medicines abruptly can be dangerous. If you have severe symptoms, such as trouble breathing or facial swelling, seek emergency care now.

prompt: What is 17% of 200? Just give the number.
